claims.statement: Ronald Reagan was born on February 6, 1911, in Tampico, Illinois, to Jack and Nelle Reagan; his older brother Neil was born in 1908.
Reagan died at his home in the Bel Air district of Los Angeles on June 5, 2004, at age 93, after a long illness with Alzheimer's disease.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without graphic detail.

claims.statement: In a letter to the American people made public on November 5, 1994, Reagan wrote that he had recently been told he was one of the millions of Americans who would be afflicted with Alzheimer's disease, and that as the disease progresses the family often bears a heavy burden.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own public disclosure; the anchor for the synthetic Alzheimer's disease and the caregiver focus.

claims.statement: Reagan's personal physicians stated in November 1994 that his annual examinations included memory testing, that over the preceding twelve months they had seen findings suggesting possible early Alzheimer's disease, and that after further testing and observation they concluded he was entering its early stages.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Physicians' public statement released with the letter.

claims.statement: Reagan was thrown from a horse in Mexico on July 4, 1989; at a routine examination at the Mayo Clinic in September 1989, doctors found fluid on his brain attributed to the fall, and it was removed surgically at St. Mary's Hospital in Rochester, Minnesota.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The source says fluid on the brain and does not name a subdural hematoma.

claims.statement: Reagan fell at home on January 12, 2001, and broke his right hip; the next day, at St. John's Health Center in Santa Monica, surgeons repaired it with a pin, plate, and screws in a 65-minute operation. He went home on January 20, 2001, and continued physical therapy at home, with no weight-bearing sessions for at least two weeks.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented anchor for the synthetic post-fracture episode.

claims.statement: Reagan survived an assassination attempt in 1981, had an operation for colon cancer in 1985, and had prostate and skin-cancer surgery in 1987.
Reagan's father, Jack, died of a heart attack on May 18, 1941, and his brother, Neil, died of heart failure on December 11, 1996.
Reagan's mother, Nelle, died on July 25, 1962, of complications of Alzheimer's disease, according to the Reagan Library.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Diagnosis in 1962 would have been clinical. A contemporary obituary is reported to give a different cause; it was not reviewed.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Reagan is a 90-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer's disease who returns two weeks after his first visit following repair of a right hip fracture, and is seen by neurology on the same day. Oxycodone and diphenhydramine were stopped two weeks ago. His hip aches a little when he walks, and scheduled acetaminophen keeps him comfortable. His caregivers report that he sleeps as well as before without the diphenhydramine and has been no more confused. He finished 35 days of enoxaparin last week, without bruising or bleeding. Home physical therapy continues, and he walks short distances in the house with a front-wheeled walker and standby help. He has had no falls. Grab bars, a raised toilet seat, and night lights went in after the home safety assessment, and loose rugs were taken up. Mild evening restlessness and repeated questions continue; a quiet, unhurried evening routine settles them. He takes donepezil each morning and vitamin D daily from a weekly organizer.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Reagan returns three months after the repair of his right hip fracture. He now walks in the house and out to the garden with his walker and supervision, and enjoys sitting outside. His hip no longer hurts, even after walking, and he has had no falls. Home physical therapy continues twice a week. His caregivers give cholecalciferol every day and report no missed doses of it or of donepezil. The evening restlessness is mild and unchanged, and the evening routine still settles it. His appetite is good, and he has gained 1 kg.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Reagan is a 90-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer's disease (FAST stage 5) who returns for his subsequent annual wellness visit, three months after his six-month review after the right hip fracture repair. He answered the health risk assessment himself, with a caregiver reading each question aloud and confirming the answers he could not recall. He has had no falls, emergency visits, or hospital stays since he went home after the operation. He walks in the house and garden with a front-wheeled walker and standby supervision. His caregivers give his medicines from a weekly organizer and report no missed doses and no new over-the-counter medicines or supplements. The evening restlessness is mild and unchanged, and an unhurried evening routine still settles it. He says he feels well and enjoys his time outdoors.

referral.question: Moderate Alzheimer's disease in a 90-year-old man one month after a fall at home and repair of a right hip fracture. Please confirm the stage, review whether donepezil is still worthwhile given his heart rate and fall risk, and advise on mild evening restlessness without antipsychotics
referral.urgency: Routine, within two weeks, on the same day as his two-week primary care check
referral.pertinent_history: Alzheimer's disease diagnosed many years ago, on donepezil 10 mg each morning. Before the fracture he walked independently but needed help choosing clothes and with all instrumental activities of daily living (Lawton IADL 1 of 8), consistent with FAST stage 5. Today MoCA 11 of 30, GDS-15 4, and Confusion Assessment Method negative for delirium. NPI-Q shows mild evening restlessness and repeated questions, with no hallucinations or aggression. Heart rate 64 with no orthostatic drop (128/70 seated, 124/70 standing); Timed Up and Go 24 seconds with a front-wheeled walker and standby help. TSH 2.3. The hospital oxycodone and diphenhydramine were stopped today; scheduled acetaminophen and enoxaparin to day 35 continue, and vitamin D was started for a level of 16 ng/mL. His caregivers' Zarit Burden Interview score is 41 of 88, and caregiver support is being arranged
questions: Do you agree that his dementia is at the moderate stage (FAST stage 5)?
Is donepezil still giving benefit, and is it safe to continue with a heart rate in the low 60s and a recent fall?
How should the evening restlessness and repeated questions be managed without antipsychotics or sedatives?
Would you add memantine now, and is any further testing needed?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Reagan, a 90-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease diagnosed many years ago, is seen at the request of Dr. Ellison six weeks after a fall at home and internal fixation of a right hip fracture. He takes part in the history as he is able, and his caregivers add detail. Since the hospital oxycodone and diphenhydramine were stopped two weeks ago he sleeps as well as before and has been no more confused. In the evenings he is mildly restless and asks the same questions again; a quiet, unhurried evening routine settles him. He has had no hallucinations, aggression, low mood, fainting, or lightheadedness on standing, and no nausea on donepezil, which he takes each morning. He walks short distances in the house with a front-wheeled walker and standby help and has had no further falls
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Ellison's first-visit assessment two weeks ago: MoCA 11 of 30, Lawton IADL 1 of 8, Barthel Index 55, GDS-15 4, NPI-Q, a negative Confusion Assessment Method, Timed Up and Go 24 seconds, and seated and standing blood pressure; TSH, blood count, electrolytes, calcium, and kidney function from the same visit; and today's Barthel Index

assessment.assessment: FAST stage 5 is confirmed: he needs help choosing clothes and with all instrumental activities, in keeping with a MoCA of 11. The course and examination fit Alzheimer's disease; there are no hallucinations, parkinsonism, or focal signs to suggest another cause. By his caregivers' account he is back to his usual cognition since the sedating hospital medicines were stopped, and there is no delirium
Worth continuing. Heart rate 62 with no fainting, no orthostatic drop, and no nausea or weight loss. Stopping a long-standing cholinesterase inhibitor at this stage can bring a noticeable decline

Mild and settled by routine, with no hallucinations or aggression. Antipsychotics would add risks of falls, stroke, and death in dementia, and sedatives and anticholinergic drugs would add falls and confusion, so none is indicated

Memantine is an option at the moderate stage, but adding a medicine during recovery from the fracture is best avoided; revisit at the yearly review. The diagnostic workup was done when the disease was first diagnosed, TSH is normal, and there are no new neurologic signs, so no repeat brain imaging or laboratory workup is needed. At the moderate stage he is outside the eligibility range for anti-amyloid therapy

recommendations: Continue donepezil 10 mg each morning; check the pulse at each visit, and reduce or stop it if the heart rate falls below 50 or he faints
Keep the quiet evening routine, with daylight and activity during the day and short, calm answers to repeated questions
No antipsychotic, benzodiazepine, or sedating antihistamine for the restlessness; if it worsens, look first for pain, constipation, infection, or a new medicine
Do not add memantine for now; revisit it at the yearly dementia review
No repeat brain imaging or further laboratory workup unless there is an abrupt change
MoCA, FAST stage, and ADL and IADL scores yearly, and a neuropsychiatric screen at each visit, on the CMID schedule
Walker and standby help for all walking, and supervision at night, because the dementia adds to his fall risk
Continue the home health aide, weekly respite, and Alzheimer's Association support services for his caregivers
